name: English Learners and Newcomers
blurb: In a trial with 217 second graders learning English, most of them Latino, a computer tutor taught the vocabulary of science and social studies units. Students who used it learned more of the taught words than students who did not, with an effect of 0.38 (Baker et al., 2020).
title: English Learners and Newcomers
answer: In a trial with 217 second graders learning English, most of them Latino, a computer tutor taught the vocabulary of science and social studies units. Students who used it learned more of the taught words than students who did not, with an effect of 0.38 (Baker et al., 2020).

papers.title: Generative artificial intelligence as a semiotic mediator in the learning of Spanish as an additional language in Secondary Education
papers.finding: Quasi-experiment, 48 immigrant secondary students, 8 weeks: GenAI with teacher mediation and guided home-language use improved academic literacy, pronunciation, and motivation.

papers.title: Effectiveness of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in language teaching
papers.caveat: Pooled effects hide variation; many studies outside the US.
papers.finding: Meta-analysis, 46 EFL studies 2022 to 2025: g = 0.74, strongest for vocabulary; larger for younger K-12 learners; works as a supplement, not a replacement; did not build self-regulation.

papers.title: Utilization of AI-aided vocabulary teaching in K-12: A case study
papers.finding: Grade 1 EFL, 20 per group, 10 weeks: AI-generated picture cards beat paper cards on post-tests, but the advantage vanished on a delayed test.

papers.title: Translanguaging within and across learning settings: A systematic review focused on multilingual children with a migration background engaged in content learning
papers.caveat: Review quality depends on included studies.
papers.finding: 94 publications: maps how home languages support content learning and the policy barriers of monolingual norms.

papers.title: Evaluating Language Models Using Linguistic Variations in Multilingual Learners' Writing: A Teacher Study
papers.venue: International Conference of the Learning Sciences
papers.finding: Teachers found a multilingual language model misread common linguistic variations in multilingual learners' writing.

papers.title: Teaching with ChatGPT as a linguistically responsive tool for multilingual learners
papers.venue: Technology in Language Teaching and Learning
papers.finding: Observations of 42 US K-12 teachers: ChatGPT used to communicate, differentiate, and scaffold multilingual learners; gaps in assessment and reflection.

papers.title: I Can Speak: improving English pronunciation through automatic speech recognition-based language learning systems
papers.venue: Innovation in Language Learning and Teaching
papers.finding: 117 Indonesian high school students, 5 weeks: both speech recognition systems improved pronunciation; detailed phonetic feedback beat general feedback.

papers.title: Error-preserving Automatic Speech Recognition of Young English Learners' Language
papers.finding: Standard speech recognition trained on adult native speech transfers poorly to children learning English and smooths over their errors, so it cannot give accurate correction without child-specific tuning.

papers.title: The effectiveness of automatic speech recognition in ESL/EFL pronunciation: A meta-analysis
papers.caveat: Pooled effects hide variation; many studies outside the US.
papers.finding: 15 studies: speech recognition pronunciation practice g = 0.69; explicit corrective feedback and practice with peers work best; practice alone and short use show small or no benefit; strongest for adults.

papers.title: Exploring an AI-based writing Assistant's impact on English language learners
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.finding: AI writing assistant (AI KAKU) for adult EFL learners reduced low-level writing load; preliminary results useful for learners needing structure.

papers.title: Bringing Assessment-to-Instruction (A2i) Technology to Scale
papers.finding: Scaled literacy technology redesigned for English learners, K to 3: mixed results; English learners in grades 2 and 3 with weaker reading benefited most.

papers.title: Effects of educational technology on reading achievement for Chinese K-12 English second language learners: A meta-analysis
papers.caveat: Pooled effects hide variation; many studies outside the US.
papers.finding: 35 studies, 7,989 K-12 students: d = 0.37 overall; comprehensive models d = 0.60; supplementary add-on activities d = 0.05.

papers.title: The impact of intelligent personal assistants on adolescent EFL learners' speaking proficiency
papers.finding: 88 ninth graders, 10 weeks: talking with a voice assistant that showed text and graphics improved speaking more than audio-only or teacher-and-peer practice.

papers.why: Voice assistants can support speaking practice.
papers.title: A case study of using Alexa for out-of-class, self-directed Japanese language learning
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.finding: Six adult learners used Alexa for self-directed Japanese practice; Alexa understood over 80% of commands.

papers.title: Technology-Assisted Vocabulary Learning for EFL Learners: A Meta-Analysis
papers.venue: Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness
papers.caveat: Pooled effects hide variation; many studies outside the US.
papers.finding: 45 studies, preschool to college: technology-assisted vocabulary learning had a large effect (g = 0.845) and helped long-term retention.

papers.title: Improving Outcomes for English Learners Through Technology: A Randomized Controlled Trial
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: RCT, 221 middle school English learners in a US urban district: individualized language practice software produced larger oral and listening gains than regular curriculum alone.

papers.title: Empowering learners of English as an additional language: translanguaging with machine translation
papers.finding: Focus groups with 28 pupils and interviews with 14 teachers in five secondary schools: learners use machine translation flexibly and critically across all stages of English development.

papers.title: Development and promise of a vocabulary intelligent tutoring system for Second-Grade Latinx English learners
papers.venue: Journal of Research on Technology in Education
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: Cluster RCT, 217 second-grade Latinx English learners: vocabulary tutor improved knowledge of taught science and social studies words (ES = 0.38).

papers.title: The effects of technology-integrated classroom instruction on K-12 English language learners' literacy development: a meta-analysis
papers.caveat: Pooled effects hide variation; many studies outside the US.
papers.finding: Meta-analysis, 42 samples, 4,354 K-12 English learners: technology-integrated literacy instruction had a medium effect (ES = 0.47) over instruction without technology.

papers.title: To Google Translate or not? Newcomer Latino communities in the middle
papers.finding: Vignettes show machine-translated school notices backfiring with Spanish-speaking families; proposes a readability checklist before translating.

children.name: The Legal Ground
children.blurb: Schools still have legal duties to English learners even though federal guidance was rescinded in 2025.

children.name: Access to Grade Level Content
children.blurb: Access to grade level content means giving English learners versions of the same material that keep the key ideas and vocabulary but simplify the language, so they can learn the subject rather than being shut out by reading difficulty.

children.name: Vocabulary and Practice
children.blurb: Vocabulary practice is the area where technology has the strongest evidence for helping English learners, with adaptive tools and individualized software adding practice time that a single teacher cannot provide to every student.

children.name: Speaking and Pronunciation
children.blurb: Voice tools can give English learners more speaking practice than a busy classroom allows, and they show real promise for pronunciation when students also get explicit corrective feedback and peer practice.

children.name: Translation and the Planned Fade
children.blurb: Live translation lets a newcomer follow a lesson from the first day, but the support should be planned to fade as English grows.

children.name: Writing Support
children.blurb: Writing support for English learners uses AI as a language resource while the student does the writing, with the teacher shaping when and how the tool and the student's home language are used together.

children.name: Checking AI Feedback Before Students See It
children.blurb: AI feedback on English learners' writing can mislead, because language models may misread features of multilingual writing as errors or miss real ones, and AI detectors frequently misclassify non native English speakers' writing as machine generated.

children.name: Newcomers
children.blurb: Newcomer students arrive with very different schooling histories and must adjust to a new language, school system and culture all at once, so their first weeks set the tone for how they feel about school.

children.name: Families, Heritage Speakers, and Home Languages
children.blurb: English learners' families and heritage speakers bring language assets that schools should treat as strengths, not deficits.

children.name: Tracking Growth
children.blurb: Tracking growth means monitoring English learners' progress in both language proficiency and content learning, using tools like proficiency growth charts to see whether a student is advancing through English levels at a healthy pace.

children.name: English Learners With Disabilities
children.blurb: Some English learners also have disabilities, and separating a language difference from a disability is one of the hardest judgments in education.

children.name: Assessing English Learners Fairly
children.blurb: Assessing English learners fairly means separating what a student knows from how well they read English, because a test can fail a capable student for language reasons rather than content reasons.

children.name: Supporting Teachers of English Learners
children.blurb: Most English learners are taught by teachers who are not language specialists, so AI can help those teachers draft supports like sentence frames, glossaries, and simplified texts.

sections.body: This section is about the two jobs English learners carry at once, learning grade level content in math, science and history while also learning the English it is taught in, and about where AI fits into that work. The book describes AI helping on both fronts, from vocabulary practice and pronunciation to writing support and translation, but only when it is used with a plan. It reports that the research here is stronger than in many areas of the Volume, especially for vocabulary, and that the legal ground under all of this shifted in 2025. The chapter covers language access for content learning, vocabulary and practice tools, speaking and pronunciation, writing support, newcomer orientation, and the cautions around translation and AI feedback.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: What works, as the book finds it, is AI used as a supplement rather than a replacement, with teacher mediation and guided home language use, and with explicit corrective feedback and peer practice in pronunciation work. What does not work is practice alone, short use, and tools that smooth over children's errors or misread their linguistic variations, and the book notes that AI did not build students' ability to manage their own learning. The rule it holds to is that access and growth must both be protected, so translation and other supports must fade over time by plan rather than becoming a permanent crutch. It also holds that a bilingual person reviews translations of academic materials and important documents, that AI feedback on English learners' writing is checked, and that AI detection is never used to judge their work.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages fit together as one chain from rights to daily practice to oversight. The Legal Ground sets the obligations, Access to Grade Level Content and Vocabulary and Practice carry the core of content learning, and Speaking and Pronunciation and Writing Support cover the productive skills, with Checking AI Feedback Before Students See It guarding the feedback loop and Translation and the Planned Fade naming the failure pattern of the permanent crutch. Newcomers and Families, Heritage Speakers, and Home Languages address orientation and the role of home languages, while Tracking Growth, Assessing English Learners Fairly and English Learners With Disabilities cover measurement and fairness, and Supporting Teachers of English Learners closes the chain. A teacher would go to the practice pages for what to do in class, a leader to the legal, tracking and fade pages for the plan and the data, and a parent to the newcomer, family and assessment pages for how their child is welcomed, supported and judged.
